title: Fast Index, Slow Cortex?: Complementary Learning Systems, Sleep Replay, and Hippocampal Consolidation on Trial — From patient H.M. & Marr's archicortex to McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly's 1995 connectionist solution to catastrophic forgetting; Wilson & McNaughton's 20x compressed place-cell sleep replay & Girardeau/Buzsáki's closed-loop sharp-wave ripple suppression; Kumaran, Hassabis & McClelland's 2016 AI experience-replay & REMERGE synthesis; adversarial stress-tests from Nadel & Moscovitch's Multiple Trace Theory, Tse & Morris's 48-hour flavor-place schema assimilation & Sharon, Moscovitch & Gilboa's cortical Fast Mapping; connectionist interference & multi-trace survival math plus spotting CLS in disguise

teenKit.tldr: Your brain uses two entirely different memory engines—a fast tracker for single experiences and a slow processor for long-term facts—to stop you from forgetting everything you learn.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how your brain replays memories while you sleep unlocks the secret to mastering new skills, studying smarter, and designing better artificial intelligence.
keyTakeaways: The brain faces a mathematical crisis called 'catastrophic forgetting,' where learning new information instantly wipes out old data if handled by a single system.
The hippocampus acts like a high-speed camera, instantly capturing one-off events like where you parked your car this morning.
During deep sleep, the brain plays back these experiences at 20x speed, slowly transferring them into the neocortex for permanent safe-keeping.

vocab.meaning: The brain's clever strategy of splitting memory into a fast, temporary recorder and a slow, permanent archive.
A seahorse-shaped structure deep in your brain that acts as an instant-replay camera for daily episodes.
The neural phenomenon where your brain races through the day's events at high speed while you snooze to lock them into long-term memory.
A fatal flaw in basic AI and neural networks where learning a brand-new fact completely erases previously stored knowledge.

quiz.question: Why would a single-system memory network struggle to learn like a human?
options: It would run out of physical space in the skull.
It would suffer from catastrophic forgetting, overwriting old memories every time it learned something new.
It would require too much oxygen to function properly.
It would only be able to remember things that happened at night.
quiz.explanation: A single-system network updating continuously would overwrite previous patterns, destroying old memories to accommodate new ones.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of the hippocampus during the memory formation process?
options: To slowly integrate facts over years of practice.
To instantly capture one-shot episodic memories like where you parked your car today.
To block out all sensory information while you sleep.
To control the motor functions required for driving.
quiz.explanation: The hippocampus is specialized for rapid, pattern-separated storage of single experiences without needing thousands of repetitions.

quiz.question: What happens to your memories inside your brain while you sleep?
options: They are completely erased to free up space for the next day.
They are compressed and replayed at high speed to train the slow neocortical memory system.
They remain entirely locked inside the hippocampus forever.
They are translated into different languages.
quiz.explanation: During slow-wave sleep, the brain reactivates neural firing patterns at high speed to transfer memory traces into the permanent neocortical archive.
